newsitem.title: JAPAN: Pre-tax rush pushes Japan car imports to record.
newsitem.headline: Pre-tax rush pushes Japan car imports to record.

text.p: A rush to buy new cars before Japan raises its consumption tax later this year pushed up sales of foreign cars in January to a record for the month, car industry officials said on Thursday.

The increased sales, particularly of British-made and German models, came despite a decline in demand for imports of Japanese brand cars made overseas, which are included in the country's overall vehicle import statistics.

This fall reflects recent moves by some carmakers to repatriate production capacity, bucking a long-standing trend for Japanese carmakers to do more of their manufacturing overseas, car industry officials said.

The Japan Automobile Importers' Association (JAIA) said on Thursday that domestic sales of imported vehicles in Japan rose 4.1 percent in January from a year earlier to 24,178 units, surpassing the previous January record of 23,235 set last year.

Volkswagen and Rover increased their numbers while sales of imported Japanese brand cars fell just over 35 percent to 4,200. Toyota Motor cars fell around 80 percent to 340 and imported Honda Motor cars fell 42 percent to 2,269.

Kunihiko Ono, the association's vice-chief secretary, said a surge in demand before Japan raises its consumption tax in April was likely to boost the full-year figures for car imports, despite an expected drop after the tax increase.

"We may see a decline in April, May and June but Japan's overall sales of imported vehicles are expected to reach 450,000 units this year," Ono said. "This is because of hefty demand ahead of a rise in Japan's consumption tax from April 1." The tax is to rise to five percent from three percent.

For years, Japanese carmakers have been locating production capacity overseas to ease the burden of the strong yen, cut overheads and move closer to markets, but signs have emerged of a shift back to Japan.

Toyota Motor's unit in Kentucky stopped making the Scepter station wagon in June last year because of poor demand in the United States. It introduced the Japanese-made Camry Gracia station wagon in Japan in December as the successor to the Scepter wagon.
Honda is expected to move production of its popular Accord Wagon to Japan from its Ohio plant this summer because of a shrinking U.S. market for station wagons.
Volkswagen topped the list of foreign car sales with 3,368 cars, up 31.9 percent from a year earlier, followed by Mercedes-Benz with 2,970, up 15.9 percent.
Adam Opel, the German unit of General Motors sold 2,736, up 8.9 percent, and Rover rose 90.9 percent to 1,590.
Imports of commercial vehicles rose sharply, helped by demand for U.S. minivans in line with a boom in Japan in recreational vehicles, Ono said.
January sales of imported commercial vehicles rose a steep 79.4 percent from a year earlier to 2,072 units.
